summary:
Cameroon criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 347-1 of the penal code, which provides for up to five years' imprisonment. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, and Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise them; reporting places Cameroon among the states in Africa with the highest prosecution rates, and a 2020 assessment described the country as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any other.

A separate statute, the Law on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime (Law No. 2010/012, Article 83(1)), criminalises online same-sex sexual propositions with one to two years' imprisonment and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse followed.

No legal gender recognition procedure, name-change route or identity-marker process is documented in the sources, and there is no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation.

Appearance alone has served as the basis for prosecution. In November 2011 a Cameroonian court jailed Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome for five years after they were seen wearing women's clothes and ordering Baileys, with the original judge citing their dress, speech and the drink as proof that they were gay. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013; defence lawyer Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcomed the acquittal. Arrests on effeminacy or appearance grounds under the colonial-era sodomy law carry sentences of six months to five years.

In February 2021 two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a Douala restaurant for wearing women's clothing and convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification, receiving five years each. On 12 May 2021 a Douala court imposed the five-year term plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs (about $370) on each, the maximum statutory term, with an appeal filed; both had been detained since February 2021 and spent five months in prison before release pending appeal. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu called the judgment a political decision with no proof of acts. Shakiro, a trans activist with a substantial online following, subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.

Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance and served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison. Three young men were sentenced to five years in November 2011 for oral sex in a parked car.

Human Rights Watch reported a documented uptick of violence against LGBTI people in 2022: since 9 March that year, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, and gendarmes beat two detainees. The organisation's senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi stated that the criminalisation law lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence.

Detention carries additional risk. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as hell, and few lawyers are willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases.

Official hostility is documented alongside these prosecutions. The US Department of State's 2010 human rights report recorded harassment and extortion of gay and lesbian people by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extort. In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, drawing criticism from the state communication council for privacy invasion, while President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy and continued prosecuting people accused of homosexual activity. In July 2010 the Minister of Communication, Issa Tchiroma Bakary, argued that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that 'he is not the only gay person in Cameroon' after the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum.

On 30 June 2024 President Biya's daughter, Brenda Biya, came out as a lesbian on Instagram, prompting a national backlash and hope among LGBTQ Cameroonians.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 penal code sits within a wider environment in which beatings of gay and transgender people in public are reported as common, and the US Department of State's 2010 report placed discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prison conditions and arbitrary arrests.

In May 2005 the government threatened medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity among 11 men arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy, an instance of coercive contact with health services rather than care.

Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organisation, was forced to shut down after a police raid, removing a service base from the community; the loss of that organisation and the reluctance of lawyers to take these cases narrow the practical protection available to residents and visitors alike.

Cameroon's criminalisation places it among the 31 African countries that outlaw same-sex relations, a regional pattern that shapes how neighbouring jurisdictions treat cross-border movement and asylum claims by LGBTQ people from the country.

Outbound asylum material shows the receiving side of the same regime: a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the United Kingdom Border Agency in August 2011 after an international airline refused to carry him, and in May 2012 the same agency sought to return an asylum-seeker it found had produced 'no credible evidence' that he was gay. These are foreign procedures, not Cameroonian entry rules.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same Article 347-1 exposure as visitors, and the identification charge used against Shakiro and Patricia shows that failure to carry identification can be added to anti-homosexuality counts in the same judgment.

The cybercrime statute reaches residents' online conduct directly: same-sex sexual propositions made online carry one to two years' imprisonment and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse followed.

Cameroonian activists have built substantial audiences discussing trans life on Facebook and YouTube, but the same platforms expose them to the prosecutions documented above; Shakiro's case ended in exile rather than resolution of her appeal.

The 2006 publication of names by tabloids demonstrates that outing through the press has been a live risk for prominent residents, occurring alongside a presidential call for privacy and continued prosecutions.

The closure of Alternatives-Cameroon after a police raid removed a community service base, and the scarcity of lawyers willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases shapes what residents can expect if charged.

The June 2024 coming-out of the president's daughter produced both backlash and hope among LGBTQ Cameroonians, indicating a contested domestic climate rather than a settled one.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cameroonian visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure for LGBTQ travellers is described in the sources; whether such a rule exists is unresolved here. The nearest material concerns outbound asylum decisions made by the United Kingdom, which are foreign procedures.

No Cameroonian border or carriage screening procedure is set out. Whether travellers are screened on arrival for gender presentation or perceived sexual orientation is not sourced.

The sources document no legal gender recognition, name-change or identity-marker procedure; whether any administrative route exists outside these sources is unresolved.

Healthcare, HIV and medication access for transgender visitors is not described in the inventory. The only health-adjacent finding is the 2005 threat of coercive medical examinations used against detained men.

No contemporary youth, school or minor-specific legal policy is documented, and nothing on trans-youth travel, medication or education targets appears in the sources.

The disposition of Shakiro and Patricia's appeal after their 2021 conviction is not stated beyond the filing of the appeal and their release pending it.
